lessons.title: Case Study: How Demographic Shifts Reshaped Japan's and China's Equity Markets

children.text: The last lesson gave you a screening framework. This one gives you the receipts: two real markets, decades apart in their demographic journey, where the shift from a young, growing population to an aging one visibly rotated which sectors and companies led the stock market. Japan's rotation has already fully played out. China's is playing out right now, in real time.
Japan: From Export Manufacturing to a Deflation-Era Value Retailer

Japan's pre-1990 bubble-era market was led by banks, real estate developers, and export manufacturers, the classic beneficiaries of a rising working-age population and a booming, credit-fuelled economy, exactly the dividend-era leadership this course's framework would predict. What replaced that leadership after the crash is the more interesting part of the story.

body.title: Japan's Market Leadership, Before and After the Turn

events.title: Banks, real estate, and export manufacturers lead
events.description: Classic dividend-era leadership, riding a rising working-age population and cheap credit into the bubble peak.

events.title: Banks and real estate collapse
events.description: The bad-loan crisis covered in an earlier lesson devastates the bubble-era leaders, wiping out much of the market's previous leadership in a single decade.

events.title: Value retail and convenience stores rise
events.description: Fast Retailing, the parent of Uniqlo, builds a large business on affordable, functional clothing suited to a frugal, deflation-era consumer. Convenience store chains like Seven-Eleven Japan and Lawson thrive as shrinking household sizes favour small, frequent purchases over large weekly grocery trips.

events.title: Automation and robotics compound
events.description: Industrial robotics makers like FANUC and Yaskawa Electric benefit directly from the labour-shortage response covered in the Japan aging lesson.

events.title: Corporate governance reform reshapes capital returns
events.description: Japan's Stewardship Code and Corporate Governance Code push listed companies toward higher dividends and buybacks, partly to satisfy an aging domestic shareholder base increasingly prioritising income over growth.

body.text: The convenience store point is easy to miss but genuinely instructive: it is not a demographic story about age directly, it is a demographic story about household size. As Japanese households shrank, average grocery baskets shrank with them, and a retail format built around small, frequent, nearby purchases outcompeted the large-format supermarket model built for bigger, less frequent household shopping.

children.text: Japan's Corporate Governance Pivot: Paying Out to an Aging Shareholder Base

Japan's 2014 Stewardship Code and 2015 Corporate Governance Code, part of Abenomics' structural reform arm, pushed listed companies to hold less idle cash and return more capital through dividends and buybacks. This reform did not happen in a demographic vacuum. An aging population increasingly relying on accumulated savings and retirement income, exactly the second-dividend savings pool covered earlier in this course, has a structural preference for income-generating assets over pure growth stories, and Japan's market has visibly tilted toward shareholder returns in the decade since.
China: From Property Boom to Property Bust, and the Rotation to a 'Silver Economy'

China's own rotation is playing out far more compressed, and far more visibly, in real time. Through the 2000s and 2010s, property developers like China Evergrande Group and Country Garden, alongside infrastructure and bank stocks, were among the largest and most dominant names in Chinese equity markets, direct beneficiaries of the urbanisation and household-formation boom that rode China's demographic dividend, covered in earlier chapters.

body.label: China Evergrande's Default
body.context: Marked the start of a broader property sector crisis, with Country Garden also facing severe distress by 2023, unwinding much of the sector's prior dominance

body.text: China's property crisis is not purely a demographic story, heavy debt-fuelled overbuilding, the kind of rising ICOR problem flagged in the growth accounting lesson, was a major contributing factor. But a genuinely slowing pace of new household formation, downstream of the fertility decline and aging trends covered earlier in this course, removed part of the structural demand growth the sector had been built to expect indefinitely.

China's policy response has explicitly named the rotation. A 2024 State Council policy document promoted developing what Chinese officials have termed the 'silver economy', directly encouraging investment in elder-care services, geriatric healthcare, and related industries, a policy-level acknowledgement that the market's centre of gravity needs to shift toward the sectors this course's demographic framework would predict for an aging economy.

children.text: The Common Pattern: Growth to Value Rotation

columns.label: Dividend-era leadership
points: Banks, property developers, and infrastructure benefiting from household formation and credit growth
Export manufacturers riding a large, cheap, growing labour force
Market rewards growth and reinvestment over cash payouts

columns.label: Aging-era leadership
points: Healthcare, eldercare, and pharma benefiting from a rising elderly share, as covered in the sector lesson
Automation and robotics offsetting a shrinking labour force
Value-oriented, income-generating retail and consumer formats suited to smaller households and frugal, deflation-era spending
Market increasingly rewards dividends and buybacks over pure growth, reflecting an aging, income-seeking shareholder base

body.title: Predicting the Next Rotation
body.scenario: A country's working-age population share has just passed its peak and begun a slow decline, its household formation rate is slowing, and its government has just announced new subsidies for elder-care services, closely mirroring where China sits today according to this lesson.
body.prompt: Based on the Japan and China case studies in this lesson, which sectors would you expect to gain relative market leadership over the following decade, and which would you expect to lose it?
body.modelAnswer: Based on both case studies, expect healthcare, eldercare services, and pharma to gain relative leadership, mirroring both Japan's post-1990s pattern and China's explicit 'silver economy' policy push. Automation and robotics would likely gain ground as the labour force shrinks, following Japan's FANUC and Yaskawa pattern. Property developers, banks tied heavily to mortgage growth, and infrastructure plays tied to new household formation would likely lose relative leadership, as they did in both Japan after 1990 and China after 2021, since their growth models depend on a demographic tailwind that is now fading rather than building.

body.title: Quick Check: The Convenience Store Insight
body.question: According to this lesson, why did convenience stores thrive in Japan even as overall consumer spending stayed weak through much of the Lost Decades?
options: Convenience stores offered lower prices than supermarkets on every product
Shrinking household sizes shifted shopping behaviour toward smaller, more frequent purchases, a format convenience stores were built for and large supermarkets were not
The government subsidised convenience stores directly as part of Abenomics
Convenience stores are unrelated to demographics; their growth was purely a marketing success
body.explanation: The key demographic driver here was household size, not income or overall spending levels. As Japanese households shrank, average grocery needs per shopping trip shrank too, favouring a retail format built around small, frequent, nearby purchases over the large-format supermarket model designed for bigger households buying in bulk less often.

body.text: Japan already ran the experiment this course has been describing in theory, decades of it, sector by sector. China is running the same experiment now, compressed and in public view. Neither market rotated instantly or evenly, but both rotated in exactly the direction this course's framework would have predicted.

points: Japan's pre-1990 market leadership, banks, real estate, and export manufacturers, collapsed after the bubble, replaced over subsequent decades by value retail, convenience stores, automation, and eventually a shift toward higher shareholder payouts.
Convenience stores' rise illustrates a subtler demographic channel: shrinking household size, not just aging or income, reshaped Japanese retail formats.

China's property developers and banks, the dominant beneficiaries of its urbanisation-driven dividend era, have faced a severe unwinding since Evergrande's December 2021 default, driven by both debt-fuelled overbuilding and a genuinely slowing pace of new household formation.
China's 2024 'silver economy' policy push is an explicit, government-level acknowledgement of the same growth-to-value, dividend-to-aging sector rotation Japan experienced decades earlier.

Both case studies show the same pattern: dividend-era leadership in banks, property, and exporters gives way to aging-era leadership in healthcare, automation, and income-generating businesses, exactly as this course's framework would predict.
